Therefore, one should not grasp onto the law <note>original: 法, dharma; referring to the teachings or phenomena</note>, nor should one grasp onto what is not the law. For this reason, the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Thus Come One; a title for the Buddha</gloss> often says: "You monks, know that the law I speak is like the analogy of a raft. If even the law should be abandoned, how much more so that which is not the law?"

### Section 7: Nothing Attained, Nothing Spoken

Subhuti! What do you think? Has the <term>Tathagata</term> attained <term>Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>Unsurpassed Complete Enlightenment</gloss>? Has the <term>Tathagata</term> spoken any law?

Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed law called <term>Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term>, nor is there any fixed law that the <term>Tathagata</term> can speak. Why is this? The laws spoken by the <term>Tathagata</term> can neither be grasped nor spoken; they are neither the law nor not the law. Why so? Because all worthy and holy ones are distinguished by <term>unconditioned laws</term> <gloss>wuwei fa; laws that are uncreated and beyond cause and effect</gloss>.

### Section 8: Arising from the Law

Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled three thousand great thousand worlds with the seven treasures <note>traditionally gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, red pearls, and cornelian</note> to give as <term>charity</term> <gloss>dana; the practice of giving</gloss>, would the merit obtained by this person be great?

Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? Because this merit does not have the nature of merit; therefore, the <term>Tathagata</term> says the merit is great.

If there is another person who receives and maintains even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it to others, their merit would surpass the former. Why is this? Subhuti! All Buddhas and the laws of the Buddhas' <term>Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> all come from this sutra. Subhuti! What is called the "Buddha-law" is not the Buddha-law.

### Section 9: One Mark is No Mark

<summary>This page explains that Buddhist teachings are like a raft to be discarded after use and emphasizes that true enlightenment cannot be captured in fixed words. It also asserts that sharing even a small portion of this sutra generates more merit than vast material wealth.</summary>
